- intent aliases or trigger records that recognize the real operator wording;
- capability ownership IDs and links;
- workflow/skill references that state when they load;
- implementation metadata or nearby registry records that identify the owning capability;
- artifact and validator links that expose the proof boundary;
- lightweight backlinks so an agent arriving at an implementation resource can recover the owning route.

Prefer registry/schema fields and validators over repeated prose when the repository already treats routing as machine-readable. Do not move deterministic behavior into Markdown. Do not create a second capabilities registry, trigger family, skill catalog, composition graph, or artifact registry merely to support this use case.

PROGRESSIVE-DISCLOSURE COMPATIBILITY
Keep the route cheap to enter. The 50k/orientation layer should identify the domain or routing entrypoint, the 30k layer should reveal the capability and its dependencies, and the task/workflow layer should load the exact skill, implementation, artifacts, and validator required. Do not preload every participating document merely to prove that links exist. Route first; load detail on demand.

INTENT OVER FILENAME
The acceptance path must not depend on the agent already knowing an internal filename. Filenames may be canonical destinations, but discovery begins from user intent or from a resource the agent has already encountered. Avoid instructions equivalent to 'go read obscure/path/file.ext' unless the repository first exposes why that path is the authoritative destination for the selected use case.

REVERSE-OWNERSHIP QUESTIONS
When an agent lands on a participating script, manifest, validator, prompt, workflow, or capability record, the routing system must let it answer:
- Why does this resource exist?
- What capability or supported use case owns it?
- What user intent leads here?
- What other resources participate in the same path?
- What validator, artifact, or evidence proves the path works?

If one of those answers requires guessing, the reverse route is incomplete. Repair the smallest canonical owner rather than pasting explanatory prose into every implementation file.

FAILURE MODES TO REJECT
- giant indexes that embed every workflow or skill;
- docs-only hooks with no executable or machine-checkable owner where the repository supports one;
- new prompt identities that duplicate an existing canonical route;
- multiple capabilities claiming the same primary use case without explicit precedence;
- orphan scripts or validators that cannot identify their owning route;
- trigger aliases that point to stale or nonexistent IDs;
- circular links that never reach implementation or proof;
- a route that works only because the implementing agent already knew the repository layout.

PROVE BOTH DIRECTIONS
Add or extend the closest routing validator/regression. At minimum exercise two representative traversals:
A. INTENT-FIRST: give a fresh-agent fixture only the desired use case. Prove it reaches the canonical capability, workflow/skill, implementation, expected artifact, and validator without a pre-supplied implementation filename.
B. IMPLEMENTATION-FIRST: begin from one participating implementation-side resource. Prove it resolves back to the owning capability and originating intent, then reaches the related participants and proof.

Fail closed on broken IDs, unresolved links, duplicate primary ownership, or a route that terminates before proof. Keep evidence versioned to the exact repository head and rerun affected traversal proof if routing owners move.

DELIVER
Report the use case, canonical routing owner, forward route, reverse route, files or registry records changed, focused validator/test, representative traversal results, unresolved ambiguity if any, and commit/PR/integration state. Keep the report compact. The success condition is that the repository guides the next agent to the right place without requiring the explanation again.

prompts.name: Outlook Work-Evidence Harvester
prompts.copy_content:
SEARCH OUTLOOK FOR BOUNDED WORK-CONTEXT EVIDENCE. DO NOT TURN MAILBOX SEARCH RESULTS INTO PAID HOURS OR FINAL TASK ALLOCATION.

SEARCH REQUEST
Period: [month/date range]
People / aliases: [names, spellings, addresses]
Project / workstream: [project or `resolve from context`]
Target claim or task family: [deployment, configuration, testing, logistics, support, etc.]
Existing ledger or destination, if supplied: [path/file/record]

MISSION
Search Outlook for messages that can support, challenge, or refine the requested work context. Keep this task bounded to evidence discovery and normalization. Do not generate the final billing workbook here.

PASS 1 — DIRECT SEARCH
Search the requested period using the supplied people, project terms, target task terms, known subjects, and obvious aliases. Read enough thread context to determine what the message actually establishes. Retain only messages that materially affect the requested claim or task classification.

PASS 2 — DELIBERATE RECOVERY PASS
Search again before finishing. Expand only the bounded vocabulary around the first-pass hits: participant/address variants, nearby thread replies, project aliases, and task synonyms such as deploy/deployment, configure/configuration, install, test, field work, support, pickup/drop-off, inventory, or other terms actually suggested by the request. Check adjacent messages in a relevant thread when needed to avoid misreading a request as completion. The second pass is required even when the first pass found useful evidence.

EVIDENCE BOUNDARY
- Attendance/roster trackers remain the authority for worked dates, paid-hour totals, and the overall billed-hour envelope when the current workflow defines them that way.
- Outlook messages are supporting task/work-context evidence. They can establish that work was discussed, requested, assigned, reported, coordinated, or completed when the message actually says so.
- A message, attachment, or linked artifact does not automatically outrank Outlook/Teams context merely because it is a file. Preserve source roles instead of inventing one universal evidence ranking.
- A request, plan, assignment, reassignment, or staffing discussion is not proof that deployment occurred.
- Task allocation can evolve. When a finding may imply later redistribution or reallocation, mark it as a candidate for reconciliation rather than silently rewriting prior billing categories.
- Do not infer hours, quantities, sites, devices, completion, or billing categories that the source does not support. Use REVIEW/UNKNOWN rather than manufacturing certainty.

NORMALIZED OUTPUT
Return one concise record per retained message with: source=Outlook; timestamp/date; sender; relevant recipients; subject/thread; durable message ID/link when available; supported fact; evidence state DIRECT or INFERRED; candidate billing category or REVIEW/UNKNOWN; redistribution/reallocation candidate YES/NO with reason; and a short note describing what the message does and does not prove. Preserve short quotations only when they materially improve traceability.

HANDOFF
Deduplicate repeated thread evidence and summarize the strongest support per claim without erasing contradictory messages. Keep the normalized findings as evidence input. If the operator asks for a new Neuron Track Hours version or billing workbook from these findings, hand the records to the existing P74 `Neuron Track Hours Billing Artifact Builder`; do not create a second artifact-builder workflow or mutate paid-hour totals inside this harvest step.

DELIVER
Report search scope, pass-1 hits, pass-2 additions/corrections, normalized retained records, unresolved contradictions, redistribution candidates, and the exact evidence set handed to the next stage.

prompts.name: Teams Work-Evidence Harvester
prompts.copy_content:
SEARCH MICROSOFT TEAMS FOR BOUNDED WORK-CONTEXT EVIDENCE. DO NOT TREAT CHAT ACTIVITY AS PAID HOURS OR ASSUME THAT AN ASSIGNMENT MESSAGE PROVES COMPLETED DEPLOYMENT.

SEARCH REQUEST
Period: [month/date range]
People / aliases: [names, spellings, handles]
Chats / channels, if known: [direct chat, group chat, channel]
Project / workstream: [project or `resolve from context`]
Target claim or task family: [deployment, configuration, testing, logistics, support, etc.]
Existing ledger or destination, if supplied: [path/file/record]

MISSION
Search Teams for messages that can support, challenge, or refine the requested work context. Keep this task bounded to evidence discovery and normalization. Do not generate the final billing workbook here.

PASS 1 — DIRECT SEARCH
Search the requested period across the relevant direct chats, group chats, and channels using supplied people, project terms, target task terms, and obvious aliases. For each candidate, inspect enough surrounding replies or nearby messages to determine whether the message records a request, plan, assignment, status update, coordination event, or completed work.

PASS 2 — DELIBERATE RECOVERY PASS
Search again before finishing. Expand only within the selected people/project/time boundary using participant variants, thread replies, project aliases, and task synonyms such as deploy/deployment, configure/configuration, install, test, field work, support, inventory, pickup/drop-off, handoff, or other terms actually suggested by the first pass. Re-open relevant threads where a later reply may confirm, contradict, or reclassify an earlier message. The second pass is required even when the first pass found useful evidence.

EVIDENCE BOUNDARY
- Attendance/roster trackers remain the authority for worked dates, paid-hour totals, and the billed-hour envelope where the current workflow assigns them that role.
- Teams messages are supporting task/work-context evidence. They may confirm work context when the message itself supports the claim, but message volume or presence does not create hours.
- Outlook, Teams, and attached artifacts each have source roles; do not invent a universal ranking where an attachment automatically outweighs communication evidence.
- Requests, plans, assignments, reassignments, staffing moves, and task handoffs are not proof of completed deployment unless later evidence establishes completion.
- Task allocation can be revised over time. If a message suggests that work should be reallocated or redistributed, flag it as a candidate for reconciliation rather than silently rewriting the billing ledger.
- Do not infer hours, quantities, sites, devices, completion, or billing categories absent from the source. Use REVIEW/UNKNOWN where the record is insufficient.

NORMALIZED OUTPUT
Return one concise record per retained message/thread with: source=Teams; timestamp/date; author; chat/channel/thread identity; durable message ID/link when available; relevant participants; supported fact; evidence state DIRECT or INFERRED; candidate billing category or REVIEW/UNKNOWN; redistribution/reallocation candidate YES/NO with reason; and a short note stating what the message does and does not prove. Include only the surrounding context needed to prevent a misleading interpretation.

HANDOFF
Deduplicate repeated chat evidence and preserve contradictions or later corrections. Keep the normalized findings as evidence input. If the operator asks for a new Neuron Track Hours version or billing workbook from these findings, hand the records to the existing P74 `Neuron Track Hours Billing Artifact Builder`; do not create a second artifact-builder workflow or change paid-hour totals inside this harvest step.

DELIVER
Report search scope, pass-1 hits, pass-2 additions/corrections, normalized retained records, unresolved contradictions, redistribution candidates, and the exact evidence set handed to the next stage.

prompts.name: Lua Flagging + Host Enforcement Repair Loop
prompts.copy_content:
BUILD OR HARDEN A LUA-FLAGGED, HOST-ENFORCED COMMAND SAFETY LOOP. DO NOT TREAT LUA AS THE PROCESS OWNER, AND DO NOT SEND A BAD AGENT-GENERATED COMMAND TO THE USER JUST BECAUSE ONE VALIDATOR PASS COMPLETED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Agent command surface: xyz_agent_command_surface
Host language/runtime: resolve from the product and repository; do not assume one.
Representative bad command or incident: xyz_bad_command_or_incident

MISSION
Catch brittle, malformed, wrong-shell, unsafe, or non-portable agent-generated commands before execution or user handoff. Reuse the repository's existing Lua embedding/readiness contract when one exists. Lua owns dynamic inspection and structured flagging; the host language owns validation of Lua results, raising/blocking behavior, retries, cleanup/rollback, execution authority, and the final decision to continue or escalate.

ARCHITECTURE BOUNDARY — HOST STAYS IN CONTROL
- Read the current Lua/host contract first. In Triage-compatible repositories, prefer the existing `lua-embedding-readiness` doctrine rather than inventing a second Lua architecture.
- Lua detects and classifies command defects. It returns structured findings; it does not own the host main loop, process lifetime, native side effects, rollback, or critical cleanup.
- The host language validates the finding schema and raises or returns the repository-native typed failure/nonzero result for blocking findings. A Lua error, malformed Lua result, or checker failure is itself a host-visible validation failure; never silently treat it as PASS.
- Keep the Lua sandbox default-deny. Do not grant shell, filesystem, network, OS, native-module, or arbitrary host-call access merely so the checker can inspect text.
- Do not pretend a Lua runtime or host adapter exists when repository evidence says it is only designed or partially implemented. Build contracts, fixtures, validators, and a product-lane implementation only where current scope and runtime support it.

STRUCTURED FLAG CONTRACT
Reuse an existing schema if present. Otherwise define the smallest versioned result shape needed by the host, with fields equivalent to:
- rule_id
- severity
- category
- shell_or_language
- location or span
- evidence
- host_action
- remediation_hint
- retryable
Keep the contract deterministic and machine-readable. The host must reject unknown required shapes, impossible severities, or malformed findings rather than guessing.

COMMAND CLASSES TO EXERCISE
Derive rules from repository doctrine and real incidents instead of inventing a universal shell style guide. Include representative fixtures where applicable for:
- wrong-shell syntax, such as Bash constructs emitted for a PowerShell or CMD operator path;
- quoting, escaping, interpolation, command-substitution, pipe, redirection, and multiline defects;
- platform/path assumptions that contradict the selected execution profile;
- swallowed or unpropagated exit codes and failure conditions;
- unbounded destructive or broad mutation commands where repository policy requires a bounded form;
- commands that bypass canonical launchers, guards, manifests, or safe wrappers without evidence;
- partial snippets that cannot satisfy the requested operation as written;
- valid counterexamples that resemble risky syntax but are correct in the declared shell.
Do not turn subjective style preferences into blocking rules. Every blocking rule needs an evidence-backed failure mode and at least one valid counterexample where practical.


OPERATOR OBSERVABILITY / TERMINAL-LIFETIME CONTRACT
Classify execution as INTERACTIVE_PASTE, TRANSIENT_CONSOLE, CHILD_PROCESS, or AUTOMATION_CI. Closing the terminal before stdout/stderr/status inspection is a defect.
- INTERACTIVE_PASTE / CHILD_PROCESS: no top-level `exit` or process-kill just to propagate failure; preserve status and keep the parent shell alive.
- TRANSIENT_CONSOLE: if inspection is needed, save exit code first, then use a native wait (`pause`/`cmd /k`, PowerShell `-NoExit`/`Read-Host`) and show status/log evidence.
- AUTOMATION_CI: never wait for human input; propagate nonzero status and durable logs.
Waits are inspection aids, not error handling. Intentional session end must preserve evidence first.

HOST ENFORCEMENT
For each Lua finding, define the host behavior explicitly:
- PASS: continue only when the structured result is valid and no blocking finding exists.
- WARN: preserve the diagnostic and continue only when repository policy permits.
- BLOCK: prevent execution/handoff, raise the native host failure, preserve rule ID/evidence/remediation context, and return control to the repair loop.
- CHECKER_FAILURE: fail closed in the host with a distinct diagnostic; do not reinterpret validator failure as a clean command.
The host owns cleanup, rollback, timeout, resource release, exit-code propagation, and durable evidence. Lua reports policy findings; the host enforces them.

MULTI-PASS REPAIR LOOP
Run deliberate bounded passes:
SCAN -> LUA FLAGS -> HOST BLOCK/RAISE -> AGENT REPAIR -> REVALIDATE.
Pass 1 must reproduce the representative bad command and prove that Lua flags it and the host refuses it.
Pass 2 must inspect the repaired command plus nearby failure classes and valid controls. Do not stop because the originally observed string changed.
Continue until a bounded fixed point: no practical blocking finding, malformed checker output, missed applicable failure class, broken valid control, or safe in-scope improvement is exposed by current evidence.
If a repair creates a new flag, consume that evidence in the next pass. Never weaken the Lua rule, host exception, fixture, or validator merely to obtain green output.
Record the flag set and disposition by pass so later agents can tell what was caught, repaired, superseded, or intentionally allowed.

AGENT AUTONOMY / USER-ONLY GATE
Keep agent-capable work with the agent. Inspect code, fixtures, shell/profile contracts, tests, validators, logs, and generated command artifacts yourself. Repair and rerun checks yourself when tools and authority permit.
Do not ask the user to choose between technically equivalent safe implementations, copy diagnostics between tools, inspect files the agent can read, or manually validate a command the agent can test safely.
Escalate only when progress truly requires user-controlled credentials, protected or physical runtime access, explicit authorization/consent, an irreducible product preference, or another action the agent cannot perform. When escalation is necessary, present the exact surviving flag/gate, what has already been tried, and the smallest concrete user action that unlocks the next pass.

VALIDATION
Use the strongest safe layers available:
1. schema/contract validation for Lua findings;
2. Lua checker fixtures and negative/positive cases;
3. host-language tests proving BLOCK and CHECKER_FAILURE become real host failures and PASS remains runnable;
4. shell/profile-specific syntax or parser checks where available;
5. integration tests proving generated command -> Lua inspection -> host enforcement -> repair/retry;
6. live/runtime proof only when explicitly authorized and necessary.
Do not claim command safety from Lua-only tests when the host raise/block path is untested. Do not claim live execution proof from static parsing.

DELIVER
Implement or repair the smallest canonical Lua/host enforcement surface rather than adding a competing checker. Report:
- existing architecture owner reused;
- Lua flag schema/rules;
- host enforcement mapping;
- representative bad and valid fixtures;
- repair passes and findings closed;
- tests/validators actually run;
- files, commits, PR/integration state;
- proof level and proof ceiling;
- remaining user-only gate, if any.
A green result is valid only when the Lua detector and host raiser agree on the same command outcome and the bounded repair loop has completed a deliberate second-pass review.

prompts.name: Failure-Class Generalization & Repository Audit
prompts.copy_content:
GENERALIZE THE FIELD FAILURE. FIX THE CLASS, NOT ONLY THE STRING THAT FAILED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Observed defect/evidence: xyz_defect_or_incident
Affected entrypoint: xyz_entrypoint_if_known

MISSION
Turn one real defect into a bounded failure-class audit. Reproduce or evidence the defect, identify the underlying boundary assumption, enumerate the nearest meaningful states that share that assumption, search the repository for analogous reachable instances, repair proven gaps, and add regressions that close the class without cargo-cult rewrites.

1. START FROM EVIDENCE
- Preserve the exact failing input, stack/error, runtime, shell/interpreter, platform, state, and entrypoint when available.
- Distinguish root cause from surface symptom. Name the assumption that failed: null/empty handling, process-output contract, locale parsing, path/environment assumption, partial write, stale state, retry/idempotency, cleanup masking, upgrade transition, privilege/context, network transition, serialization drift, concurrency, or another evidence-backed class.
- Do not invent a universal checklist. Select only states plausible for this boundary.

2. BUILD A FAILURE-STATE MATRIX
For the selected class, include the nearest meaningful cells. Typical cells are:
- ordinary success;
- empty or null success;
- malformed or unexpected shape;
- partial/interrupted result;
- ordinary failure;
- silent failure or missing diagnostics;
- retry/re-entry/idempotent repeat;
- old-state -> new-state upgrade;
- concurrent or privilege/context variant when relevant.
Mark each cell PROVED, FAILING, NOT APPLICABLE, or UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is not PASS.

3. AUDIT ANALOGOUS REPOSITORY BOUNDARIES
Search for the dangerous idiom or assumption across the repository. Examples: direct dereference after native commands, nullable `.Trim()`/property access, optional JSON fields, unchecked registry/environment reads, locale-sensitive parsing, partial-state cleanup, stale cache/state, unchecked exit codes.
For every candidate: inspect reachability and contract before mutation. Reject false positives explicitly. Do not blanket-replace syntax merely because it resembles the incident.

4. REPAIR + REGRESS
- Fix the smallest canonical owner for each proven reachable gap.
- Add the observed failure as a regression.
- Add the nearest meaningful adjacent cells that would fail for the same reason.
- Preserve valid counterexamples so the fix does not over-block legitimate behavior.
- If the class crosses components, add integration proof at the actual boundary, not only helper-unit coverage.

5. SECOND PASS
After green tests, inspect the diff and matrix again. Ask: `What adjacent state could still fail for the same underlying reason?` Search once more for analogous reachable occurrences. Convert concrete gaps into another repair pass. Do not manufacture churn when the bounded matrix is actually closed.

6. AUTONOMY
Run searches, tests, fixtures, validators, and safe repairs yourself. Do not send the user hunting for code or reproducing checks the agent can perform. Escalate only a genuine user-only credential, protected runtime, physical action, authorization, or irreducible product decision.

DELIVER
Report: observed defect; failure class; state matrix and dispositions; analogous candidates inspected; repairs; regressions; tests run; proof ceiling; remaining UNKNOWN cells; commit/PR/integration state.

CLOSURE RULE
A test proving the reported input is fixed is necessary, not sufficient. Close the defect class only when the nearest practical adjacent states and reachable analogues are either proved, repaired, not applicable with evidence, or explicitly left as gaps.

prompts.name: Canonical Path Prompt
prompts.copy_content:
ESTABLISH AND ENFORCE THE CANONICAL DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION PATH FOR THIS REPOSITORY. DO NOT LET AGENTS OR HUMANS INVENT A NEW LOCATION BECAUSE ANOTHER PATH IS CONVENIENT.

Repo/app: xyz_repo_or_app
Machine/profile: xyz_machine_profile_or_resolve_from_evidence
Observed current path, if any: xyz_current_path_or_unknown
Observed production/use entrypoint, if any: xyz_entrypoint_or_unknown

MISSION
Give the repository one durable, machine/profile-aware answer to `Where do we develop it?` and `Where do we run/use it?` Encode the resolution rule in the harness so agents, scripts, launchers, and operators derive the same locations instead of scattering clones, worktrees, installs, or partial app copies. Remote repository completion is not local workstation deployment.

1. REFRESH TRUTH BEFORE CHOOSING A PATH
- Refresh remote/default-branch truth and read current governance, harness maps/contracts, machine/profile routing, launchers, installers/updaters, and worktree conventions.
- Inspect the actual current working directory and bounded known checkout/install candidates when observable.
- Never invent a literal user path from model preference, another machine, remembered chat, or a convenient Desktop/AppData/OneDrive location. Remembered paths are evidence to verify; tracked repository/profile contracts own the durable rule.

2. DEFINE PATH ROLES
For each supported machine/profile record:
- CANONICAL DEVELOPMENT CHECKOUT — normal writable Git checkout.
- CANONICAL PRODUCTION / USE PATH — installed, synchronized, served, or operator-facing location.
- CANONICAL WORKTREE ROOT — optional isolation root; temporary worktrees are not alternate canonical checkouts.
- CANONICAL ENTRYPOINT — launcher/command/script that consumes the use path.
- PATH RELATION — whether development and production are the same location or require explicit sync/install/promotion.
Do not collapse roles merely because one machine currently shares a directory.

3. CODIFY ONE AUTHORITY
Reuse an existing machine/profile/path registry or contract. Otherwise add one owner in the repository's existing harness convention and make it discoverable from the harness entrypoint. Do not standardize a filename across repositories or create a second path authority.
Encode repository identity, profile key, path-resolution rule, development/use/worktree roles, entrypoint, and precedence. Use variables where portability requires them; do not commit secrets or person-private evidence. Wire the owner into existing doctor/preflight, intake, launcher, updater/sync, resolver, worktree helper, validation profile, or status flow where applicable.

4. PREVENT PATH SPRAWL AND COMPUTER BLOAT
Before clone/install/worktree/CD instructions, resolve the canonical rule and classify observed locations as CLONE, WORKTREE, INSTALL, MIRROR, CACHE, OUTPUT, or BACKUP. Refuse a second normal mutable checkout when the canonical one is usable; isolate parallel writers under the approved worktree root.
Inventory noncanonical copies before cleanup. Preserve dirty, unpushed, unique, or separately owned work. Never force-reset or delete merely to make the machine tidy.

5. ENVIRONMENT-DERIVED MACHINE / PROFILE PATH RESOLUTION
Canonical is one repo-owned rule per profile, not one literal string. Build a PATH INPUT RECEIPT from current evidence: OS/platform and path semantics; native home/profile source; actual OS special-folder locations used by the rule; allowed machine/profile override; OneDrive/cloud root and target-folder state when relevant; verified checkout evidence; and material symlink/junction/mount/drive/case behavior. Username/account is runtime input, never a portable constant.

For OneDrive/cloud state distinguish NOT_APPLICABLE, ABSENT, ROOT_AVAILABLE, ROOT_UNAVAILABLE, TARGET_FOLDER_REDIRECTED, MULTIPLE_ROOTS, and UNKNOWN as applicable. An installed/running client is not proof Desktop/Documents are redirected. If the rule says `Desktop\Dev`, resolve Desktop through the OS; on Windows do not assume `%USERPROFILE%\Desktop`, and do not rewrite it under OneDrive unless the actual Known Folder location is redirected there. Ambiguous roots/redirection -> CONFLICT/UNKNOWN. An unavailable canonical root is a blocker, never permission for silent fallback or a second clone.

Resolution precedence: tracked canonical-path/profile contract -> authorized machine/profile override -> native home/special-folder/environment resolution -> verified existing-checkout evidence. Lower-precedence evidence may expose drift but may not silently replace the owner. If current host and target profile differ, route/handoff rather than fabricate a target path locally.

5A. EXECUTION CONTEXT RECEIPT BEFORE PATH-SENSITIVE COMMANDS
When command syntax, path semantics, launcher behavior, or agent/tool availability depends on execution context, record the terminal surface/host, actual shell/interpreter, kernel/OS/runtime boundary, execution target (local, WSL, container, VM, SSH/remote, or CI), and material path/filesystem semantics. A terminal application is not the shell, and a shell prompt does not prove the kernel/runtime or target. If these facts materially affect the next mutation and cannot be recovered, set `EXECUTION_CONTEXT=UNKNOWN` and do not emit a guessed shell-specific or target-specific write command. If host and target differ, route/handoff or use an explicitly target-scoped invocation.

5B. DEVELOPMENT MUTATION VS ACTIVE PRODUCTION USE
Production/use path is a consumer path, not the default development mutation target. Record `PROD_USE_STATE` as ACTIVE, QUIESCED, OFFLINE, or UNKNOWN from current evidence. ACTIVE includes a process, service, launcher, server/watcher, scheduled job, sync/updater, operator session, or other consumer that can observe the path. UNKNOWN is not idle: it blocks production-path mutation while safe development work may continue.
- When development and production are separate, edit/build/test only in the canonical development checkout or approved worktree, then cross the tracked sync/install/update/promotion boundary. Do not copy a partially built tree into production or use ad-hoc file edits as deployment.
- When development and production resolve to the same physical path, record that relation explicitly. Any write is production-impacting; do not call it a dev-only change. Either the tracked contract must prove in-place mutation is safe for the current use state, or isolate development before changing files.
- Do not `git pull`, reset, rebuild, overwrite, or regenerate files in an ACTIVE production/use path merely because it is local. When consumers could observe files mid-update, use the repository-native safe boundary: quiescence, staged/atomic or versioned replacement, restart/reload coordination, or an equivalent mechanism that prevents partial candidate state. Do not invent a deployment mechanism when the repository already owns one.
- After promotion/update, resolve the production version from the real entrypoint and preserve the repository-defined restore/rollback path when the update can fail after mutation.

6. FAIL CLOSED ON PATH DRIFT
When identity matters, a mismatch must report canonical rule/path, observed path, attempted role, evidence source, and exact safe next action. Use CANONICAL + PROVED, NONCANONICAL + PRESERVE, NONCANONICAL + DISPOSABLE, MISSING, CONFLICT, or UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is not permission to guess.

7. REMOTE INTEGRATION IS NOT LOCAL DEPLOYMENT
Track separately:
- REMOTE_INTEGRATED — intended commit is contained in refreshed remote default branch.
- DEV_CHECKOUT_CURRENT — canonical development checkout contains the required integrated commit and is safely reconciled.
- PROD_PATH_CURRENT — canonical production/use path consumed the required version through its real mechanism.
- ENTRYPOINT_PROVED — real operator entrypoint resolves the canonical production path and observes intended behavior.
A GitHub merge proves only remote integration. Updating the dev checkout does not prove a separate install/use path was refreshed.

8. MAP BOTH PATHS WHEN TEST PROOF IS INVOLVED
After location identity is proved, compare:
A. REAL: operator action -> canonical production/use path -> launcher/wrapper -> shell/interpreter -> config/environment -> services/native boundaries -> result.
B. TEST: test runner -> checkout/fixture/helper -> exercised boundaries -> assertions.
Mark material boundaries SAME + PROVED, SAME + WEAKER INPUT, SIMULATED/MOCKED, BYPASSED, PRODUCTION-ONLY, or UNKNOWN. Green helper tests do not prove a production wrapper, installed copy, or workstation path they never invoked. Use same-entrypoint synthetic proof when live execution is unavailable but the real launcher can be exercised safely.

9. SECOND PASS — TRY TO CREATE THE BUG AGAIN
Ask:
- Could another agent entering fresh still choose a different directory?
- Could OS/user/home, Desktop Known Folder, OneDrive redirection, mount/junction, or profile state make the same logical rule resolve differently?
- Could a launcher use a stale install while remote main/dev checkout are current?
- Could an ACTIVE or UNKNOWN production consumer observe files while development, sync, build, or update mutates its path?
- Could development and production resolve to the same physical directory so a supposedly dev-only write is actually live?
- Could the terminal host mask a different shell, kernel/runtime, execution target, or path semantics and make the next command wrong?
- Could a parallel agent create a second mutable checkout?
- Could a mirror/cache/backup be mistaken for source authority?
- Could a resolver silently fall back when canonical evidence is missing?
Add the smallest practical regression for concrete gaps; stop at a bounded fixed point.

10. DELIVER
Report the PATH INPUT RECEIPT/resolution source; material EXECUTION CONTEXT RECEIPT; PROD_USE_STATE; canonical development/use/worktree paths and their physical relation; owning contract/resolver and dev-to-production promotion/update boundary; noncanonical-copy disposition; remote SHA; local/prod/entrypoint proof; files/commit/PR/integration state; and exact blocker for any uninspected machine.

CLOSURE RULE
Close only when future agents/operators can derive the same development and production locations from repository-owned evidence, environment-dependent literals resolve reproducibly without hard-coded usernames, path drift is blocked or diagnosed, unique work is preserved, ordinary mutation stays in development unless a same-path production-safe contract is proved, active production cannot observe partial candidate state, and remote integration is no longer confused with local deployment.

prompts.name: Use-Case Closure Certification
prompts.copy_content:
CERTIFY THE USER-FACING USE CASE. TRY TO PROVE THE CLOSURE CLAIM FALSE BEFORE CALLING IT CLOSED.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Use case / original request: xyz_use_case
Claim being certified: xyz_done_working_closed_claim

MISSION
Turn a vague completion claim into observable acceptance obligations. Gather current evidence, mark gaps honestly, attack the weakest assumptions, repair exposed in-scope defects, and certify only the proof level that survives a deliberate falsification pass. This is user-facing closure certification, not merely a clean PR or a polished final report.

1. RECONSTRUCT THE CLAIM
Recover what the user actually expects to be able to do. Translate `works`, `done`, `deployed`, `fixed`, or equivalent language into concrete observable obligations: entrypoint, inputs, outputs, state changes, failure behavior, persistence, permissions/context, compatibility, restore/cleanup behavior, and any explicit no-regression constraints.
Do not add requirements the request never implied. Do not drop inconvenient requirements because implementation already exists.

2. BUILD THE OBLIGATION LEDGER
For each material obligation record:
- obligation;
- owning surface;
- evidence;
- status: PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN / NOT APPLICABLE;
- proof level;
- next falsification or repair action.
UNKNOWN is not PASS. `No known bug` is not evidence. A merged PR proves integration, not necessarily the operator use case.

2A. CHECK FAITHFULNESS BEFORE FETCHING MORE
When an agent authored the claim, pin the authoritative truth and the relevant generation context when recoverable. Classify a material mismatch as FACTUALITY_MISSING_CONTEXT (needed truth absent), FAITHFULNESS_CONTEXT_IGNORED (truth/instruction present but ignored, contradicted, or materially underused), ATTENTION_SATURATION (required truth present inside distracting/overgrown context), MIXED, or UNKNOWN.
A confident, plausible, good-faith answer can still fail closure. Missing context calls for targeted retrieval/grounding. If the correct information was already available, do not reflexively add more context: re-anchor to the smallest authoritative sources, compact stale/distracting material, rebuild the affected obligations, and rerun certification.


3. FALSIFY CLOSURE
Choose the weakest or highest-consequence obligations first. Exercise practical variants such as:
- first run vs repeat run;
- ordinary success vs meaningful failure;
- empty/malformed/partial input when relevant;
- old state -> new state/upgrade;
- alternate supported shell/platform/user/privilege context;
- stale state/cache/configuration;
- interruption/retry/idempotency;
- cleanup/restore;
- real launcher/entrypoint vs helper path.
Use only variants relevant to the claim. Do not create ceremonial test volume.

4. REOPEN ON EVIDENCE
If a falsification attempt fails, closure is open. Repair the smallest canonical owner, add a regression where practical, rerun affected obligations, and update the ledger. Do not preserve a green status by weakening an acceptance obligation.

5. SECOND PASS
After all material obligations are green at the claimed level, critique the ledger once more: `What could make the user reasonably say this is not actually closed?` Inspect current diff, tests, artifacts, runtime path, and known failure classes. Close concrete in-scope gaps immediately. Stop only at a bounded fixed point.

6. PROOF LEVEL
Separate: static/schema, unit/helper, integration, same-entrypoint synthetic, field/live runtime, and user-observed acceptance where those levels exist. State the ceiling. Never call synthetic proof live closure.

7. AUTONOMY
Perform repository inspection, safe tests, artifact checks, and repairs yourself. Do not ask the user to validate what the agent can verify. Ask for user participation only when closure truly depends on inaccessible credentials/runtime, physical action, explicit consent, or irreducible user-observed acceptance.

DELIVER
Claim; obligation ledger; falsification passes; gaps found and repaired; validators/tests/runtime checks; evidence still UNKNOWN; certified proof level/ceiling; commit/PR/integration state; exact blocker if closure remains open.

CERTIFICATION RULE
`CLOSED` is valid only when every material obligation is PASS or evidence-backed NOT APPLICABLE at the declared proof level and the deliberate falsification pass exposes no practical unaddressed gap. Otherwise report `NOT CERTIFIED` and continue repair when safe.

prompts.name: Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard
prompts.copy_content:
PROVE THIS CHANGE DID NOT BREAK BEHAVIOR THAT ALREADY WORKED. TEST THE NEW OUTCOME AND THE PROTECTED OLD OUTCOMES; DO NOT VALIDATE ONLY THE PATH YOU JUST CHANGED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Change / PR / commit: xyz_change_identity
Requested outcome: xyz_new_or_repaired_behavior
Known-good reference: resolve current accepted main/release/commit from evidence

MISSION
Treat regression testing as preservation proof. Establish what was already expected to keep working, determine which call stacks/contracts/state transitions the change can affect, exercise the smallest meaningful protected set before and after the change when practical, and repair any breakage without weakening the old contract just to make tests green. For runtime-facing use cases, run the canonical live path yourself when a safe environment is available.

1. PIN THE COMPARISON FLOOR
- Refresh repository/provider truth and identify the exact known-good reference and exact candidate head.
- Preserve versioned evidence: a test or live run proves only the head, inputs, environment, and entrypoint it actually observed.
- If the reference itself is already broken or ambiguous, say so and use the strongest earlier accepted evidence rather than fabricating a baseline.

2. BUILD THE PROTECTED-BEHAVIOR LEDGER
Recover behavior that the change must preserve from:
- the original/current user request and explicit non-regression constraints;
- existing focused/integration/end-to-end tests that represent real contracts;
- prior accepted runtime/field evidence, runbooks, examples, bug history, and compatibility promises;
- observable behavior at interfaces touched by the diff.
For each protected behavior record: entrypoint, input/state, expected observable result, owning contract/test, proof level, and why the current change could affect it.
Do not assume every existing test is a valuable contract. Do not let deleting or rewriting a test silently delete an accepted behavior.

3. TRACE CHANGE IMPACT THROUGH CALL STACKS
Inspect the changed symbols/files and map practical affected paths:
ENTRYPOINT -> CALLER -> ORCHESTRATION -> DOMAIN/STATE OWNER -> ADAPTER/IO -> RESULT/ERROR.
Include reverse callers and shared dependencies, schema/config migrations, caches/state, retries/cleanup, privilege/context, serialization, and concurrency only when the diff can reach them.
Use this map to select regressions. Do not run an enormous unrelated suite as a substitute for understanding impact.

3A. PROTECT COMPOSED UI STATE AND INTERACTION SEQUENCES
For interactive products, a set of individually passing controls can still form a broken journey. Add sequence-level protected controls around state that composes across actions: search query/results, active filters, focus, selection, detail/panel visibility, clipboard/completion feedback, and persisted preferences where relevant. For each action, name the state it semantically owns and the state it must leave untouched.

A visibility toggle should not erase an active search query or its matching result set unless clearing search is an explicit product contract. Likewise, a shortcut that is meant to complete a user action must be tested through that terminal outcome, not merely through an intermediate panel open. Exercise keyboard and pointer routes together when they represent the same semantic action. Keep deliberate clear/reset commands as protected counterexamples so preservation rules do not make state impossible to clear intentionally.

4. BASELINE WHEN IT ADDS SIGNAL
When safe and affordable, exercise representative protected controls on the known-good reference in an isolated worktree/build/runtime and record the result. Then run the same controls on the candidate.
If baseline execution is impractical, use durable prior evidence and current contract tests, clearly marking the lower proof level. Never pretend a historical green badge is a fresh live baseline.

5. RUN AUTOMATED REGRESSIONS
Run in dependency-aware order:
- focused tests for the changed behavior;
- focused protected controls for impacted existing behavior;
- caller/integration tests across changed seams;
- migration/upgrade/retry/idempotency tests where the change affects persisted or transitional state;
- broader suite/build/static checks when practical.
Add a regression that reproduces every concrete regression found. Keep valid counterexamples. Do not modify expected results, snapshots, fixtures, mocks, or tolerances merely to fit the broken candidate unless the product contract truly changed and that change is explicitly supported by the request.

6. RUN THE CANONICAL LIVE PATH WHEN THE CLAIM IS LIVE
If the feature is an app/browser/service/CLI/device/operator workflow and a safe executable environment exists, do not stop at synthetic tests. Use the product's canonical launcher/entrypoint and exercise:
A. the requested new/repaired behavior; and
B. at least one impacted previously working control.
Observe the actual result, not only route issuance, command ACK, process exit, or mocked output. Collect bounded evidence/logs. If live proof requires inaccessible credentials, protected hardware/runtime, destructive action, or explicit operator authorization, state the exact gate and proof ceiling; do not claim the regression closed at the live level.

7. REPAIR WITHOUT TRADING ONE BUG FOR ANOTHER
When a protected behavior fails:
- locate the smallest canonical owner;
- preserve the requested new behavior and the old valid behavior together;
- repair implementation/contract migration rather than weakening the regression gate;
- rerun the failing control plus the new feature path immediately;
- inspect adjacent callers for the same break mechanism.
If the failure generalizes into a broader defect class, use the failure-class audit pattern; if tests bypass the real production boundary, use the production-path proof-gap pattern.

8. DELIBERATE SECOND PASS
After first green:
- inspect the diff, test changes, mocks/fixtures/snapshots, impacted call stacks, and live evidence again;
- ask `What behavior could this change break that our selected tests would not notice?`;
- add or run the smallest practical missing control;
- repeat repair/revalidation for concrete gaps.
Stop at a bounded fixed point; do not manufacture test volume.

9. AUTONOMY
Run the tests, worktrees, builds, launchers, fixtures, logs, and safe live checks yourself when tools permit. Do not make the user a regression runner or evidence courier. Escalate only a genuine inaccessible runtime/credential/physical/authorization gate.

DELIVER
Report: reference fixed point; candidate head; protected-behavior ledger; impact/call-stack map; automated regressions run; live controls run; regressions found/repaired; before/after evidence; tests added/changed; second-pass result; proof level/ceiling; remaining blocked controls; commit/PR/integration state.

ROUTING BOUNDARY
- Use failure-class auditing when one regression exposes a reusable defect class.
- Use production-path proof-gap auditing when tests and the actual execution path differ.
- Use the dedicated live-runtime executor for a deeper protected runtime proof sprint.
- Use closure certification only after preservation and requested behavior are both proved at the claimed level.

prompts.name: Program Design & Call-Stack Prototype Architect
Stateful Socratic Technical Tutor Workspace
prompts.copy_content:
TEACH THIS TOPIC AS A STATEFUL, SOCRATIC TECHNICAL WORKSPACE. DO NOT DUMP A STATIC GUIDE OR SOLVE THE HARD PARTS FOR ME BEFORE I HAVE A CHANCE TO PRACTICE THEM.

Repo/topic: xyz_repo_or_topic
Mastery goal: recover from the current conversation or ask only if genuinely absent
Teaching workspace: use the repository-local `.teach/` protocol. If its canonical core is absent, route first to Teach Workspace Protocol Bootstrapper; do not clone or install an external teaching package merely to use `/teach`.
Session invocations: `/teach <topic>` starts or resumes one topic; `/teach recap` refreshes verified prior learning.

MISSION
Help the learner build a durable mental model through first-principles decomposition, active retrieval, practical exercises, and persistent evidence of what has actually been understood. Treat teaching as a multi-session state machine rather than a one-shot explanation. Ground factual claims in repository truth and high-trust sources, preserve the learner's exact frontier, and adapt scaffolding when a concept is not yet secure. A passive guide or opaque answer is not success: the learner must be able to reconstruct the mechanism, diagnose failure, and apply the invariant without cargo-culting the tutor's output.

1. RECOVER GOAL AND STATE BEFORE TEACHING
Read the current conversation for:
- why the learner wants this skill;
- what they already understand or have attempted;
- terminology and analogies that already worked;
- misconceptions or repeated sticking points;
- desired practical outcomes;
- time/depth constraints.
If an existing teaching workspace exists, read its mission, resources, latest learning records, lessons, and reusable assets before creating anything. Do not ask the learner to repeat recoverable context.

2. REQUIRE THE CANONICAL `.teach/` CORE BEFORE A SESSION
`/teach <topic>` is a teaching-session command, not a bootstrap command. The established core is:
.teach/
  MISSION.md            # current topic, target outcome, constraints, frontier
  RESOURCES.md          # ground-truth repository docs/specs and trusted references
  lessons/              # numbered modular lessons or visual `.html` simulators
  learning-records/     # dated evidence of verified understanding
If this core is absent, use Teach Workspace Protocol Bootstrapper first. Do not create or clone a separate teaching repository and do not require an external package. Optional `assets/` or `reference/` material may be added later only when a lesson actually needs it. Keep tutorial state out of production code.

3. GROUND BEFORE EXPLAINING
For repository-specific facts, inspect the current code, tests, docs, contracts, examples, and runtime evidence. For external technical facts, gather high-trust primary/official sources when available. Treat unsupported model memory as a hypothesis, not a citation. Record sources compactly in RESOURCES.md or the existing authority surface. Cite the source for claims that matter to the lesson.
Prefer a small trustworthy resource set over a giant link dump.

4. DECOMPOSE FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES
Break the target skill into the smallest concepts that explain the larger system. Teach structural relationships and invariants before memorized recipes. Use concrete examples, diagrams, traces, state transitions, or call stacks when they expose mechanism.
For each concept answer:
- What problem exists?
- What primitive or invariant solves it?
- How do the pieces compose?
- What can fail or be misunderstood?
- What observable evidence distinguishes correct from incorrect reasoning?
Do not introduce five abstraction layers when one prerequisite is still unstable. Keep each lesson atomic around a single testable invariant so broad topics do not dilute context or hide which relation failed.

4A. REPOSITORY DATA-STRUCTURE GRILL MODE — USE MATT POCOCK'S `grill-me` DISCIPLINE
When the mastery goal is understanding the data structures at play in a repository, switch from broad teaching into a repository-specific grilling lane. The purpose is human upscaling: the learner should understand the structural model deeply enough to complement AI capabilities, catch bad assumptions, and review generated changes rather than becoming a passive prompt operator.

GROUND THE STRUCTURE MAP BEFORE ASKING FACT QUESTIONS
Inspect the repository yourself first. Build a compact evidence-backed map of the structures that actually matter, including as applicable:
- entities/types/classes/records and their fields or shapes;
- identity and keys, cardinality, containment, references, indexes, and graph relationships;
- ownership and lifecycle: who creates, mutates, validates, caches, persists, expires, or deletes each structure;
- schemas, serializers/deserializers, API/event/message payloads, migrations, persistence models, state stores, caches, queues, and configuration representations;
- transformations between representations and the call/data-flow seams where shape or ownership changes;
- mutability, concurrency, ordering, nullability, versioning, and other material invariants;
- tests, fixtures, migrations, and failure paths that reveal the intended model.
Do not make the learner perform repository archaeology that the agent can perform. If a question can be answered by exploring the codebase, explore it first and turn the finding into a reasoning challenge.

USE THE ACTUAL SKILL WHEN AVAILABLE; NEVER PRETEND IT RAN
If Matt Pocock's `grill-me` skill is available in the current agent environment, invoke it as the interview primitive for this lane. If it is unavailable, say `SKILL_UNAVAILABLE` once and follow the same documented discipline locally; do not claim the skill executed. Do not install tools or mutate the repository merely to obtain the skill unless the user separately authorizes that setup.

GRILL ONE DEPENDENCY AT A TIME
- Ask exactly one data-structure question at a time and wait for the learner's answer before selecting the next branch.
- Walk the dependency tree rather than following a fixed questionnaire. Resolve prerequisite concepts before downstream ones.
- Each question should include a short evidence-backed current model or recommended answer as a hypothesis for the learner to defend, refine, or reject; do not dump the full solution or remove the need for retrieval.
- Prefer questions about relationships and consequences over trivia: why a key exists, who owns mutation, where a representation changes, what invariant prevents corruption, what breaks if cardinality or ordering changes, and which boundary should reject an invalid shape.
- When the learner misses a relation, lower the abstraction, show a smaller trace or concrete instance, then ask a new one-question retrieval check.

TRACE REAL DATA THROUGH THE REPOSITORY
Before calling the structure understood, trace at least one representative datum from an entrypoint or source through validation, transformation, in-memory/state ownership, persistence or transport, and final consumer/output. Name the concrete files/types/functions that establish each hop. If the repository has multiple materially different data paths, choose another trace only when it tests a distinct ownership or representation boundary.

COMPLEMENT-AI MASTERY GATE
Do not mark this lane MASTERED merely because the learner can recite type names. The learner should be able to:
- reconstruct the important structure map without reading it verbatim;
- explain identity and keys, ownership and lifecycle, and the highest-value invariants;
- predict which structures and boundaries a proposed feature or repair is likely to touch and why;
- diagnose at least one plausible shape/ownership/invariant failure from evidence;
- challenge an AI-generated design or diff by identifying a structural assumption that must be proved against the repository.
The target is leverage: AI can search and generate quickly; the human must upscale enough to reason about the model, detect architectural drift, and make higher-quality decisions with the AI.

5. RUN A SHORT DIAGNOSTIC, THEN TEACH AT THE FRONTIER
Before a new cluster of lessons, ask a small diagnostic that reveals the learner's actual model. Do not quiz trivia for ceremony. Use the result to choose the next atomic lesson. The diagnostic is a progression gate, not decoration: if the learner cannot explain the mechanism, lower the scaffolding one level before continuing.
If the learner answers incorrectly or incompletely:
- identify the missing prerequisite or mistaken relation;
- lower the abstraction/scaffolding one level;
- give a smaller worked example or visual aid;
- ask a new retrieval question that tests the repaired concept.
Do not simply reveal the final answer and mark the topic complete.

6. END EVERY ATOMIC LESSON WITH EXACTLY TWO LEARNER CHECKPOINTS
After the first-principles explanation, halt with exactly:
A. CONCEPTUAL TRADE-OFF / MECHANISM — one question about the invariant, trade-off, causal mechanism, or failure state; and
B. CODE DIAGNOSTIC / EDGE CASE — one small exercise requiring diagnosis, a critical code fragment, test expectation, state transition, or edge-case reasoning.
Then stop and wait for the learner's response. Do not answer the checkpoint yourself in the same turn. Evaluate the response before advancing; incorrect or incomplete reasoning changes the scaffolding rather than being silently promoted to mastery.

7. ZERO BLACK-BOX PRODUCTION GENERATION DURING TEACHING
During an explicit teaching session, do not jump straight to a polished production implementation of the difficult logic the learner is trying to master. You may provide scaffolding, interfaces, fixtures, failing tests, partial code, toy examples, visualizers, and targeted hints. Let the learner fill the critical reasoning/logic when that is the learning objective.
If they explicitly switch from teaching to delivery/build mode, make that mode change clear and route production implementation separately rather than silently defeating the lesson.

8. USE TEST-DRIVEN LEARNING WHEN CODE IS THE SKILL
A strong exercise pattern is:
- tutor writes a focused failing test or incomplete harness expressing one invariant;
- learner predicts the failure and implements the smallest logic to pass;
- tutor reviews the diff for correctness, reasoning, edge cases, and production patterns;
- learner explains why the solution works and names one failure case;
- tutor records mastery only after both code and explanation support it.
Use this pattern for consequential failure modes such as concurrency bugs, memory churn, state edge cases, routing mistakes, or contract violations when they match the skill being learned. Do not write tests so broad that the learner can cargo-cult a giant solution.

9. BUILD IMMERSIVE LOCAL HTML/JS LEARNING DEMOS WHEN INTERACTION CAN CARRY THE CONCEPT
Do not treat interactive artifacts as a rare flourish. During lesson design, explicitly ask whether the current invariant would become easier to predict, manipulate, observe, or diagnose through a local demo. For algorithms, ASTs, state machines, event loops, packet routing, memory behavior, concurrency, call stacks, data structures, geometry, or other structural topics, prefer a small self-contained local HTML/JS learning lab over another page of prose when interaction materially reduces abstraction cost. Treat each learning lab as a self-contained HTML/JS visualizer whose interactions are tied to the lesson invariant, not as a generic mini-app. Store a lesson-specific demo under `.teach/lessons/<NN>-<topic>.html`; put genuinely reusable controls, renderers, fixtures, or visualization helpers in `.teach/assets/`.

IMMERSIVE DEMO LOOP — PREDICT -> MANIPULATE -> OBSERVE -> EXPLAIN
- PREDICT: before changing the demo, ask the learner what state transition, output, ownership change, call path, or failure they expect and why.
- MANIPULATE: let the learner change a meaningful input or system state with controls such as step/back/reset, sliders, toggles, data injection, drag/reorder, breakpoint or phase controls, and trace filters.
- OBSERVE: make causality visible with highlighting, traces, state snapshots, counters, diagrams, canvas renders, before/after views, or success/failure paths that expose what actually changed.
- EXPLAIN: require the learner to reconcile prediction with observation and name the invariant or mechanism before the lesson advances.

Design for active causality, not passive animation. Engagement must come from meaningful agency, visible causality, and rapid feedback rather than decorative motion or gamification theater. A good demo lets the learner perturb the model, replay or reset it, and see why the system behaves differently. Where useful, expose both a healthy path and a representative failure/edge state so the learner can diagnose rather than merely watch.

Keep demos local-first and self-contained when practical. Do not add an external build system, CDN, framework, service, or package merely to make a lesson flashy when plain HTML/CSS/JS can express the concept. Use sanitized fixtures and repository-grounded shapes; never embed secrets, private data, production credentials, or unsafe live endpoints in a teaching demo.

When creating or reusing a demo, give the learner its exact local path and launch/open command. Smoke-check that the artifact exists and is structurally loadable; when browser execution is available, exercise the primary interaction plus one reset/failure path. If browser/runtime proof is unavailable, say so and keep that interaction UNPROVEN instead of claiming the demo was observed.

Reuse components from existing `.teach/assets/` or lesson assets before creating new ones. If a new component is generally reusable, extract it into the teaching asset owner rather than inlining copies into multiple lessons. Do not build decorative UI that does not improve comprehension.


9A. OFFER MERMAID AS AN OPTIONAL STRUCTURAL LAYER
Use Mermaid when a compact declarative diagram would lower the learner's structural load without requiring a full interactive control surface. Good candidates include architecture/dependency maps, sequence/call flows, state transitions, entity/class relationships, ER-style data relationships, and data-flow or ownership boundaries. Treat Mermaid as a layer or option, not a mandatory artifact and not a substitute for the immersive HTML/JS learning lab when the learner needs to manipulate state, replay transitions, inject data, or observe causal behavior.

Choose the lightest useful representation:
- prose when the relation is already simple;
- Mermaid when the learner mainly needs to see stable relationships, order, ownership, or topology;
- interactive HTML/JS when meaningful manipulation, stepping, reset, or experimentation carries the concept;
- Mermaid plus HTML/JS only when the static map genuinely helps the learner orient before or after interacting with the demo.

Keep Mermaid evidence-grounded. Every important node, edge, state, or relationship should correspond to repository evidence, a trusted source, or the explicit toy model used by the lesson. Prefer the smallest diagram that makes the current invariant legible; do not dump an entire repository graph when one bounded slice teaches the concept better. For repository data-structure lessons, Mermaid can visualize entity relationships, ownership/lifecycle boundaries, transformation seams, or representative data flow before the learner is grilled on them.

MERMAID + SOCRATIC USE
When it improves retrieval rather than revealing the answer too early, ask the learner to predict a missing edge, next state, call hop, ownership boundary, or failure path before showing or completing that part of the diagram. Then use the diagram as evidence for the explanation checkpoint, not as a replacement for the learner's explanation.

RENDERING / PORTABILITY RULES
- Prefer fenced Mermaid source in a Markdown lesson or a colocated `.mmd`/text snippet when the environment already supports Mermaid rendering.
- Do not install a Mermaid package, add a CDN, or introduce a build/runtime dependency merely to render a teaching diagram unless the user separately authorizes that environment change.
- If the current viewer cannot render Mermaid, preserve the Mermaid source as a readable artifact and continue the lesson; do not block teaching on rendering support.
- Distinguish source proof from render proof. If the agent did not actually render the diagram, say the Mermaid source was created but visual rendering is UNPROVEN.
- Keep diagram labels sanitized and free of secrets, private data, credentials, or sensitive production values.

Do not create Mermaid for ceremony. If a diagram adds no structural insight beyond the existing prose or interactive demo, omit it.

10. VERIFY BEFORE WRITING THE LEARNING RECORD
Do not create a VERIFIED/MASTERED learning record merely because a lesson was delivered. Evaluate the learner's conceptual and diagnostic responses first. When understanding is demonstrated, write or update `.teach/learning-records/<date>_<topic>.md` with concise evidence: concept, checkpoint result, practical/edge-case evidence, remaining weak point if any, and next frontier. If verification fails, record NEEDS_REVIEW/PRACTICED only when that state is useful and continue scaffolding; never label exposure as mastery.

11. `/teach recap` — RE-ANCHOR VERIFIED WORKING MEMORY
When invoked with `/teach recap`, read `.teach/MISSION.md` plus all relevant files in `.teach/learning-records/` before teaching anything new. Build a compact refresher from concepts actually verified, then run a quick roughly three-minute quiz focused on the most important or fragile relationships. Revisit only what decayed and continue from the first unmastered frontier. Do not replay the curriculum from the beginning and do not infer mastery from a record that lacks verification evidence.

12. ITERATE THE CURRICULUM
After each lesson inspect whether the chosen decomposition worked. If the learner repeatedly fails a checkpoint, revise the lesson order, analogy, visualizer, or prerequisite rather than repeatedly asking the same question. Reuse what worked. Remove or merge lessons that duplicate each other. Keep one canonical resource/lesson owner where practical.

13. AUTONOMY AND USER AGENCY
Research facts, inspect repository evidence, maintain teaching state, build exercises/visualizers, and adapt scaffolding yourself. The learner owns learning decisions and must perform the retrieval/practice that demonstrates mastery. Do not offload fact gathering or repository archaeology to the learner when the agent can do it.

DELIVER / SESSION CLOSE
At the end of a teaching session report only what helps continuation:
- mastery goal and current frontier;
- concepts MASTERED / PRACTICED / NEEDS_REVIEW;
- diagnostic/practical evidence;
- teaching artifacts created or reused;
- sources/resources added;
- next atomic lesson;
- exact way to resume (`/teach <topic>` or `/recap` as appropriate).
The success criterion is durable understanding that survives the next session, not the volume of explanation produced.

prompts.name: Open-Source Prior-Art & Gap Analyst
Teach Workspace Protocol Bootstrapper
prompts.copy_content:
ESTABLISH OR REPAIR THE REPOSITORY-LOCAL `/teach` WORKSPACE PROTOCOL. DO NOT TEACH THE TOPIC YET.

Repo or directory: xyz_repo_or_path
Lane: teaching workspace bootstrap
Owned scope: `.teach/` core state plus the existing canonical agent-instruction surface needed to route `/teach`
Forbidden scope: production feature work, a separate teaching repository, external teaching packages, unrelated agent-rule rewrites, fabricated learning records

MISSION
Make `/teach` a pure workspace protocol that can be dropped into an ordinary repository or directory. Establish durable state and one discoverable agent rule so later teaching sessions can resume from evidence instead of reconstructing the learner's history. This bootstrap prompt owns setup only; Stateful Socratic Technical Tutor Workspace owns actual `/teach <topic>` and `/teach recap` sessions.

1. RECOVER THE LOCAL OWNER BEFORE CREATING FILES
Inspect repository policy and existing agent instruction surfaces first. Reuse the canonical owner already used by the project (for example AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, `.cursorrules`, or a repo-specific system-prompt file). If several exist, follow repository precedence rather than duplicating the `/teach` rule into all of them. Preserve unrelated instructions.

2. NO PACKAGE OR CLONE DEPENDENCY
Treat `/teach` as folders + Markdown/HTML lesson artifacts + an agent routing rule. Do not install an external dependency and do not clone or create a dedicated teaching repository merely to enable it. The target repository/directory itself owns the learning state.

3. ESTABLISH THE CANONICAL CORE
Create or repair only this required core:
.teach/
  MISSION.md            # current learning objective, target outcome, constraints, frontier
  RESOURCES.md          # ground-truth repository docs/specs and trusted references
  lessons/              # numbered modular lessons; `.html` is allowed when a visual simulator materially helps
  learning-records/     # dated records written after learning verification
Do not pre-create decorative subtrees. Preserve valid existing `.teach/` work and merge missing structure non-destructively.

4. SEED STATE WITHOUT INVENTING MASTERY
MISSION.md may contain a compact blank/current template for Topic, Target outcome, Constraints, and Current frontier. RESOURCES.md may explain how authoritative repository/spec links and notes are recorded. Do not invent completed lessons, resources, or MASTERED records. Empty directories may use the repository's established placeholder convention only when version control requires it. Treat `.teach/` as version-controlled mental documentation when repository policy and data sensitivity permit, so future maintainers and future sessions can recover the verified model alongside the code; never commit secrets, private data, or sensitive learning evidence.

5. INSTALL THE `/teach` AGENT RULE
Add a bounded rule to the canonical agent instruction owner:
- `/teach <topic>` updates `.teach/MISSION.md`, grounds the lesson from `.teach/RESOURCES.md` plus repository truth, creates/reuses `.teach/lessons/<number>_<topic>.md` (or `.html` for a useful visual), teaches from first principles, never jumps to final production code, and ends with exactly one conceptual trade-off/mechanism question plus one code diagnostic or edge-case exercise.
- The agent must stop for the learner response, evaluate it, and write `.teach/learning-records/<date>_<topic>.md` as VERIFIED/MASTERED only after demonstrated understanding.
- `/teach recap` reads the learning records first and runs a quick roughly three-minute refresher quiz before resuming at the first weak/unmastered frontier.
Keep this rule as routing/behavior policy; do not duplicate the whole tutor prompt into governance.

6. VALIDATE THE BOOTSTRAP
Use repository-native checks where available. At minimum prove the four core paths exist, MISSION.md/RESOURCES.md are readable, the canonical instruction owner contains both `/teach <topic>` and `/teach recap`, and no unintended production files changed. Run `git diff --check` and the closest docs/governance test if the repository has one.

7. CLOSE AT THE SETUP BOUNDARY
Report the instruction owner, `.teach/` artifacts created/reused, validation, any repository-specific limitation, and the exact next invocation `/teach <topic>`. Do not silently cross into the lesson itself. If a `.teach/` workspace was already complete and correctly routed, prove that and make no ceremonial churn.

prompts.name: User-Flow Friction & Preference Telemetry Refiner
prompts.copy_content:
REFINE THE USER FLOW, NOT JUST THE INDIVIDUAL CONTROL. FIX REDUNDANT INTERACTION STEPS, PRESERVE ORTHOGONAL STATE, AND USE SEMANTIC USAGE EVIDENCE WHEN PERSONALIZATION OR A MOST-USED DASHBOARD IS IN SCOPE.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Journey or friction: recover from the current conversation/runtime evidence
Primary terminal user goal: xyz_terminal_goal_or_resolve_from_evidence

MISSION
Take a user journey that technically works but feels wrong, destructive, redundant, or opaque and make the flow match the user's actual goal. Treat search text, filters, focus, selections, panels, clipboard actions, notifications, and preference data as composed state with explicit owners. Optimize the complete sequence rather than declaring each button or hotkey correct in isolation. When the user wants personalization, measure semantic completions and derive the preference surface from those events without turning every hover, view, or panel-open into fake intent.

1. REPLAY THE REAL JOURNEY
Start from the exact user entrypoint and reproduce the interaction in order. Record a compact journey-state ledger with: step, input, state before, semantic action, state after, visible feedback, and whether the step advanced the terminal goal. Include keyboard and pointer routes when both are supported. Do not replace the user's stated friction with a designer-invented journey.

2. DEFINE THE TERMINAL USER VALUE
Name what the user is actually trying to accomplish. Opening a panel, moving focus, or revealing detail is not automatically success when the real goal is to copy, execute, submit, compare, navigate, or otherwise use the underlying object. Mark intermediate UI as scaffolding, not closure. Prefer the shortest understandable route that preserves discoverability and safety.

3. PRESERVE ORTHOGONAL STATE
For every control identify which state it owns and which state it must leave alone. A visibility toggle should not clear an active search unless clearing search is part of its documented semantic contract. A panel open/close action should not destroy unrelated selections, filters, or query state. Make destructive transitions explicit. Add sequence regressions that combine controls, because isolated-key tests cannot prove composed state.

4. COLLAPSE REDUNDANT INTERMEDIATE STEPS
Find steps that merely expose a control for an action the initiating shortcut already unambiguously means to perform. If a favorite-item shortcut semantically means 'use this favorite' and the safe terminal action is copy, invoke the canonical copy action directly, reuse the normal success toast/feedback, and keep existing panel/navigation commands available separately. Do not create duplicate close/clear rituals when another supported command already owns them. Preserve accessibility and an obvious way to inspect detail when inspection is genuinely requested.

5. REPAIR THE DEFAULT INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE
Measure how much of the initial viewport is consumed before primary content as a flow-economy metric. Persistent control density is friction even when every control works. Prefer classification -> progressive disclosure -> subordinate choices; parents first, then only in-scope subcategories. A Hide/Show toggle reduces clutter on demand but does not fix a noisy default information architecture. Reuse deterministic existing classifications; preserve search, keyboard and mobile use, Favorites, and active-state semantics.

6. UNIFY ENTRYPOINTS ON SEMANTIC ACTIONS
Keyboard shortcuts, buttons, command palette items, touch controls, and automation should call the same domain-level action where they mean the same thing. Do not let one path mutate search/filter/detail state differently just because it was implemented by another listener. Keep state ownership, feedback, and error behavior centralized.

7. INSTRUMENT SEMANTIC USAGE, NOT NOISE
When personalization or usage analytics is requested, define the smallest event contract that represents meaningful completion. Examples: prompt copied, prompt executed, artifact exported, workflow completed. Do not count focus, hover, panel-open, detail-view, or failed attempts as successful use unless the product explicitly needs a separate diagnostic metric. Make increment semantics idempotent enough that one user action cannot double-count through bubbling or duplicate handlers.

8. OWN PREFERENCE DATA EXPLICITLY
Define event identity, item ID, timestamp or bucket only when needed, storage owner, schema/version, retention/reset behavior, device/profile/account scope, migration, and failure behavior. Before mutating a shared telemetry/preferences owner, confirm this journey is authorized to own that schema or contract change; otherwise reuse the existing owner and route the shared-owner change separately instead of expanding scope implicitly. Prefer local/private storage for local-only personalization unless the product already owns authenticated sync. Never collect prompt bodies, secrets, clipboard contents, or other sensitive payloads merely to count usage. Provide a clear reset/export path when that matches existing portability patterns.

9. DERIVE THE DASHBOARD FROM EVENTS
If an interactive most-used/preferences dashboard is in scope, derive it from the canonical aggregated event store. Show useful dimensions only: usage count, recent use, favorite status, category/type, or trend when supported by actual data. Let users filter/sort/drill into the same canonical prompt/item identities. Do not hard-code rank order or maintain a second preference truth. Empty/new-user state must be useful and honest.

10. TEST SEQUENCES AND FAILURE STATES
Add focused tests for the actual compositions that failed or could fail:
- active search -> unrelated filter show/hide/toggle -> query and matching results preserved;
- favorite shortcut -> terminal action occurs once -> normal success feedback appears -> no unnecessary detail panel required;
- pointer and keyboard versions of the same semantic action produce equivalent state and telemetry;
- storage failure does not fake a successful preference write;
- duplicate event dispatch does not double-count one completion;
- reset/migration preserves the documented boundary;
- dashboard derives from stored usage and updates after a qualifying action.
Protect existing deliberate clear/reset/navigation behaviors as controls.

11. MEASURE FLOW ECONOMY
Compare before/after using concrete interaction evidence: steps/keystrokes, focus changes, unnecessary panel transitions, destructive state resets, time-to-terminal-action where practical, and qualitative operator friction already supplied. Do not optimize for fewer clicks when the removed step carried necessary safety, confirmation, or comprehension.

12. LIVE-PATH PROOF
Run the canonical browser/app path when safely available. Reproduce the original friction, execute the repaired sequence, observe actual clipboard/notification/state/dashboard behavior, and run at least one protected neighboring path. Static tests prove contracts; they do not prove browser focus, clipboard permissions, event ordering, or rendered-dashboard behavior. State the exact proof ceiling when the live path is inaccessible.

DELIVER
Report the original journey, terminal goal, destructive/redundant steps, state-owner changes, semantic event contract, privacy/storage boundary, dashboard derivation, before/after flow evidence, focused sequence tests, live proof, commit/PR/merge state, and any remaining product-only decision.

ROUTING BOUNDARY
Use the generic Prototype-Measure-Refine loop when the main problem is broad experimentation rather than user-flow friction. Use Program Design & Call-Stack Prototype Architect when module/state ownership itself is still unresolved. Use Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard to protect already accepted behaviors around the change. This prompt owns the product-flow repair plus preference-telemetry/dashboard slice when those concerns are coupled by the user journey.

prompts.name: Factuality vs Faithfulness Hallucination Diagnoser
prompts.copy_content:
DIAGNOSE THE HALLUCINATION BEFORE TRYING TO FIX IT. MISSING KNOWLEDGE AND IGNORED KNOWLEDGE REQUIRE DIFFERENT FIRST RESPONSES.

Agent/model surface: xyz_agent_or_model_surface
Failed output / claim: xyz_failed_output
Authoritative truth: xyz_source_of_truth
Generation context: recover when available

MISSION
Turn `the agent hallucinated` into an evidence-backed failure classification. Determine whether the model lacked the required information, had the information but failed to follow it, or was operating in context so noisy/large that present constraints were not reliably reflected in the output. Then repair the cause and rerun the same bounded case. Do not diagnose hidden chain-of-thought or pretend output text reveals internal attention directly.

1. PIN THE FAILURE AND TRUTH
Select one concrete wrong, invented, contradictory, or materially incomplete claim, code decision, identifier, parameter, or completion assertion. Pin the authoritative source that establishes the expected result. Separate correctness from style or preference.

2. RECOVER WHAT WAS ACTUALLY AVAILABLE
Reconstruct the relevant generation-time context when possible: system/user instructions, source excerpts, retrieved files, tool results, schemas, prior summaries, and other material that could reasonably govern the disputed output. Search it directly for the required fact/constraint. Do not assume the model `must have known` something merely because it exists in training data or elsewhere in the repository.

2A. VERIFIER ROLE INTEGRITY GATE
When the active request asks P100 to validate, audit, review, or challenge another agent's output, preserve that verifier mission. This gate does not convert an explicit prompt/policy-design request into candidate auditing.
